questions.q: Two threads run `count++` on a shared `int` without synchronisation. Why can updates be lost?
o: The increment is read, add, write, so threads can overwrite each other
The JVM lets only one thread touch an int at a time
Integers are immutable, so the write is ignored
The garbage collector resets the value between threads
questions.w: `count++` is three steps, not one atomic action. Use `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder` or a lock.

questions.q: What does the `volatile` keyword guarantee for a field?
o: Writes are visible to other threads, but compound actions stay non-atomic
Every method touching the field becomes synchronized
The field is held in a faster CPU register only
The field can no longer change after construction
questions.w: `volatile` gives visibility and ordering for single reads and writes. `volatile int x; x++` is still a race.

questions.q: What is the main difference between `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock`?
o: `ReentrantLock` adds timeouts, interruptible waits and fairness
`synchronized` works across several JVMs, `ReentrantLock` does not
`ReentrantLock` releases itself at the end of the block
`synchronized` can guard only a single variable
questions.w: `ReentrantLock` must be unlocked in a `finally` block. Prefer `synchronized` for simple cases and a lock when you need its extra features.

questions.q: Two threads each hold one lock and wait forever for the other's lock. What is this called, and what is the standard prevention?
o: Deadlock; always acquire locks in one global order
Livelock; add more threads to the pool
Starvation; raise the priority of the waiting thread
Race condition; mark both locks volatile
questions.w: Consistent lock ordering removes the circular wait. Also keep critical sections small and use timeouts such as `tryLock`.

questions.q: You submit 10,000 short tasks. Which approach is the most sensible?
o: A bounded thread pool from an `ExecutorService`
A brand new `Thread` for each of the tasks
One `synchronized` method that runs them all
A `Thread.sleep` between every submission
questions.w: Pools reuse threads and cap resource use. Unbounded thread creation can exhaust memory and slow the whole JVM.

Blocks until the future completes and returns the value
Cancels the future when it takes too long
Runs the stage again every time it is called
questions.w: It chains non-blocking steps. `get()` and `join()` are the blocking calls. Pass your own executor to avoid saturating the common pool.

questions.q: Why is `ConcurrentHashMap` preferred over `Collections.synchronizedMap` for heavy concurrent use?
o: It locks only small parts of the map, so contention drops
It keeps keys in sorted order for quicker lookups
It permits `null` keys and values to skip checks
It never needs to resize as it grows
questions.w: A synchronized wrapper uses one lock for every call. `ConcurrentHashMap` uses CAS and fine-grained locking per bin. It rejects `null` keys and values.

questions.q: A task in a thread pool throws an exception inside `Runnable.run()` submitted with `execute()`. What typically happens?
o: The worker thread dies from the exception and the pool replaces it
The exception is rethrown to the code that called `execute`
The pool shuts itself down at once
The task is silently retried three times
questions.w: With `submit()` the exception is captured inside the `Future` and only appears on `get()`. Always handle or log task failures.
